lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 4, what is a majority? (More than half of the votes.) In history this year you met Athens, where citizens voted on their own laws. Today: what democracy means, then and now.

Democracy means rule by the people. In a democracy, the people choose who makes decisions, can speak freely, and can vote those leaders out at the next election. Many countries around the world are democracies.

In Athens, citizens voted on each law themselves: that is direct democracy. Countries today have millions of people, so they elect representatives, people who make laws for them. That is representative democracy.

In an election, candidates explain their ideas, then voters choose. The vote is secret, so nobody can be pressured. The votes are counted carefully and the result is announced, and those who lose accept it.

In Athens only some men could vote, and for a long time women and many others could not vote anywhere. People campaigned for years to change that. In 1893 New Zealand became the first country where women could vote in national elections.
Turnout is the share of voters who actually vote. If 1,000 people can vote and 650 do, turnout is 65 out of 100: 65%. Every vote counts the same, so taking part matters.
Democracy works in schools too: a school council, with pupils elected by their classes, can bring ideas to teachers. Good representatives listen to everyone, not only to their friends.
Try it in the world: hold an election with your friends for a building-team captain: ideas on signs, secret votes posted into a chest, and a careful count. Next: laws.

exercises.prompt: In a democracy, who chooses the leaders?
exercises.hint: Demos is the Greek word for the whole population of a place.
exercises.explain: The people choose their leaders by voting.

exercises.prompt: In an election, the vote is secret.
exercises.hint: Why might a voter want nobody to know their vote?
exercises.explain: True: a secret vote means nobody can pressure or punish a voter.

exercises.hint: Candidates explain their ideas before the vote.
choices: someone who wants to be elected
exercises.explain: A candidate is someone who stands in an election, hoping to be chosen.

exercises.prompt: In a democracy, leaders can be voted out at the next election.
exercises.explain: True: if people are unhappy, they can choose someone else at the next election.

exercises.prompt: Where did citizens first vote on their own laws?
exercises.hint: Think of the Greek city where Cleisthenes gave citizens the vote.
Big countries cannot all vote on every law.
choices: a person elected to decide for others
exercises.explain: A representative is elected to make decisions and laws for the people who voted.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: direct or representative democracy?
items: citizens vote on every law themselves
a class votes on its trip
exercises.hint: Do people decide themselves, or choose someone to decide?
exercises.explain: Direct: every law, Athens' Assembly, the class trip vote. Representative: electing lawmakers, a parliament.

exercises.prompt: 200 pupils can vote in the school council election and 150 vote. What is the turnout, as a percentage?
exercises.hint: How many out of 100 is 150 out of 200?
Could you vote freely if someone was watching?
choices: so nobody can pressure or punish voters
exercises.explain: A secret vote lets everyone choose freely, without pressure.

exercises.prompt: In Athens, all adults could vote.
exercises.explain: False: only free men with Athenian parents could vote.

exercises.prompt: Which country first let women vote in national elections, in 1893?
exercises.hint: It is in the Pacific Ocean, far from Europe.

exercises.prompt: A candidate loses an election. What should happen in a democracy?
exercises.hint: Everyone agreed the rules before the vote.
choices: they accept the result and try again later
exercises.explain: They accept the result; they can try to win next time.

exercises.prompt: Why do big countries elect representatives instead of voting on every law?
exercises.hint: Think of millions of people meeting on one hill.
choices: too many people to vote on every law
exercises.explain: With millions of people, it is easier to elect a smaller group to study and vote on each law.

exercises.prompt: Look at the table: Tilly won more than half of all the votes.
exercises.hint: Add all the votes and find half.
exercises.explain: True: 18 + 9 + 7 = 34 votes, and half of 34 is 17. Tilly got 18, which is more than 17: a majority.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of an election in order.
exercises.hint: You cannot count votes before they are cast.
exercises.explain: Ideas, then the secret vote, then the count, then the result.

exercises.prompt: Match each election word to its meaning.
matches: the share of voters who vote
exercises.hint: Think of an election: who stands, how people vote, who turns up, and who wins.
exercises.explain: A candidate hopes to be elected. Turnout is the share of voters who vote. A majority is more than half the votes. A secret ballot means nobody sees how you voted.

exercises.prompt: 2,000 people can vote in a town election, and the turnout is 60%. How many people voted?
exercises.hint: 60% means 60 out of every 100. How many hundreds are there in 2,000?
exercises.explain: 2,000 is 20 hundreds, and 60 voted in every hundred: 20 × 60 = 1,200 people.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: a sign of democracy, or not?
items: one ruler for life, with no vote
losers refuse to accept the result
exercises.hint: Card 1: the people choose, speak freely and can vote leaders out.
exercises.explain: Democracy: leaders can be voted out, people speak freely, and votes are secret. Not democracy: a ruler for life with no vote, and losers refusing to accept the result.
